title_original: Clervaux – Cité de l’image, A Space Dedicated to Artistic Research : An Interview With Sandra Schwender
excerpt_original: An Interview With Sandra Schwender on the Clervaux – Cité de l’image Artistic Research and Programme Cet article Clervaux – Cité de l’image, A Space Dedicated to Artistic Research : An Interview With Sandra Schwender est apparu en premier sur The Eye of Photography Magazine .

blocks.text: In Clervaux, photography moves beyond exhibition walls to take over public spaces. Combining local engagement, international collaborations and support for contemporary artists, Sandra Schwender, Director of Clervaux – Cité de l’image, discusses the ambitions of this distinctive project in Luxembourg.
How did Clervaux come to be recognised as a City of Photography?

Clervaux’s development into a “City of Photography” was closely linked to the historic photographic collection The Family of Man , assembled by Luxembourgish-American photographer Edward Steichen. This internationally renowned exhibition has been housed at Clervaux Castle for more than thirty years. In recognition of its exceptional importance to photography, it was inscribed on UNESCO’s Memory of the World Register in 2003 and is managed by the Centre national de l’audiovisuel (CNA).

This major photographic collection provided the foundation for the concept of “Clervaux – Cité de l’image”. In 2008, an association dedicated to promoting and presenting contemporary photography was established through close collaboration between the CNA and the municipality of Clervaux. The aim was to connect the historical significance of The Family of Man with contemporary photographic practices and continually encourage new perspectives on the medium.

The association organised various cultural events, including exhibitions, installations, workshops and conferences. Particular attention was given to free accessible photographic installations in public spaces, presented at different locations throughout the town. Clervaux thus gradually became a place for encounters with photography, establishing itself as the “City of Photography”.
What are the different formats through which photography is presented in the town each year?

The project now has nine exhibition sites in public spaces, where photographic installations are renewed annually. Since November 2025, the Cité de l’image has also had its own exhibition space in the former Tourist Office premises. Three to four exhibitions are presented there each year.

For larger exhibitions, the CNA also makes the Brauhaus premises available. This is where, for example, the Photography Prize is held every two years. Up to two or three additional exhibitions are conceived and organised in these spaces each year.

These additional exhibition opportunities have allowed the Cité de l’image to continually expand and diversify its programme. Contemporary photography can be presented not only in public spaces but also in conventional exhibition galleries, making it accessible to a broad audience. Combining these two presentation formats opens up different possibilities for engaging audiences with photography and creates space for a variety of artistic approaches.
How do you establish connections with other organisations and institutions in the town, such as schools?

Since taking over as Director of the Cité de l’image, I have been particularly committed to establishing new collaborations with cultural organisations, institutions and partners. My priority is to strengthen its position regionally, nationally and internationally, build new networks and develop valuable synergies through joint projects.

An important, longstanding collaboration has existed with the Centre national de l’audiovisuel (CNA) since the Cité de l’image was founded. In addition, cooperation with the Lycée Edward Steichen in Clervaux has intensified over the past two years. Students specialising in photography present their own photographic work every year in the Jardin du LESC. Throughout the school year, they receive guidance from their teachers and benefit from workshops led by professional artists, which give them fresh perspectives and additional inspiration.

It is particularly important to me to introduce young people to photography from an early age, encourage their interest in the medium and provide them with a platform where they can develop and present their own creative expressions.

We have also established various collaborations at the wider regional and international levels. These include our partnership with Kultur | lx, through which the Cité de l’image was invited to participate in portfolio reviews in Arles, as well as our regular involvement in EMOP (European Month of Photography).

To offer a preview of 2027, the Cité de l’image and the CNA will jointly launch the first FOTO CLIERF photography festival, which will take place in Clervaux from June 26 to September 12, 2027. As part of Luxembourg Art Week, we intend to introduce the project to a wider audience for the first time. At our joint stand, we will provide an overview of the festival, present its concept and highlight the participating artists.
How did you approach the new season? What are its main themes and priorities?

When developing a new season of exhibitions in public spaces, I am particularly keen to address a wide range of themes. These range from political and socially critical questions to personal and conceptual approaches, as well as humorous and playful perspectives. As a general rule, I invite an artist for each exhibition site to explore a theme I have proposed and interpret it through photography.

For the 2026–2027 season, however, I deliberately chose a different approach and experimented with a new exhibition concept. Instead of inviting several artists, I decided to entrust the entire season to a single artist. I invited Austrian artist Kay Walkowiak, who took over seven exhibition sites in public spaces and also organised a workshop at the local secondary school. This approach makes it possible to develop a coherent artistic identity across the different locations.

All is but Temporary, conceived for Clervaux – Cité de l’image, brings together Kay Walkowiak’s photographic series throughout the town for an entire year. How did you work with the artist to develop the exhibition and establish connections between his work and the different spaces in the municipality?

When I contacted Kay Walkowiak last year, I proposed that he exhibit across the seven sites located in public spaces. For me, this was an experiment and a new curatorial approach. I therefore deliberately wanted to give him a kind of carte blanche , allowing him to develop his own ideas and vision freely.

After several telephone conversations and extensive discussions this exhibition format was also a first for him he eventually accepted. A few weeks later, he presented his exhibition concept. He had studied each site in depth and carefully considered which of his existing series would be most appropriate for each location. His proposals immediately convinced me, because the selection of works was highly coherent, both in terms of content and in their relationship to their respective surroundings.

His series The Mechanics of Form , exhibited in the Jardin de Lélise, is one example. These photographs depict patang kites, which fill the skies in many parts of India during the Uttarayan festival in January. Once the festivities are over, many of these kites remain caught in the treetops.

This creates a beautiful connection with the exhibition site in Clervaux. The Jardin de Lélise is characterised by a sloping landscape dotted with rocks and dense bushes. Looking at the installation, one almost has the impression that the kites have also become caught in the bushes and shrubs here. The photographic work enters into direct dialogue with its surroundings and becomes integrated into the site in its own distinctive way.

Kim Lang’s exhibition Whispers of the Sunlit Coast is also presented over an extended period on the site of a former miniature golf course. What relationship emerges between the scenes of Rio de Janeiro photographed by Kim Lang and this particular space?

This year, the brand-new Konschtpark (Art Park) has expanded our range of spaces dedicated to art and culture in the public realm. It is already our ninth outdoor exhibition site, further extending the possibilities for integrating art into people’s everyday lives.

Kim Lang is the first artist to present a photographic series there, bringing a distinctive atmosphere to the Konschtpark. His photographs, taken particularly around Copacabana Beach, convey a mood that harmonises with the character of this new location.

The Konschtpark is intended as a place of tranquillity and a slower pace of life, a space for encounters and exchanges where nature and culture come together naturally. It invites visitors to pause, become more aware of their surroundings and open themselves to art.

The Konschtpark is not simply a space dedicated to art; it is also intended as a place for strolling, somewhere where visitors can linger, discover, contemplate and perhaps escape everyday life for a moment.

Trixi Weis’s exhibition Once upon a time , which closes in a few days, translates an installation project into photography. How does the Cité de l’image approach the connections and intersections between photography and the visual arts?

Luxembourgish artist Trixi Weis has always worked across different media and recently returned to a photographic project after a long break. Precisely because photography continues to evolve and open up new possibilities for expression and creation, I find it particularly fascinating to observe how artists appropriate the medium, question it and reinterpret it within their own artistic practices.

The Cité de l’image aims to be a place where such experimentation is possible: a space dedicated to artistic research, new perspectives and innovative exhibition formats. Photography, or more precisely the image, naturally remains central, but the aim is also to create opportunities to explore the boundaries of the medium and experiment with new forms of presentation.

Last spring, Marie Capesius presented the results of two creative residencies organised at the invitation of the Cité de l’image. Could you tell us more about how this work was presented? More broadly, how do you support artists in developing new projects?

The artist residency project was a particularly rewarding and exciting collaboration, based on a partnership with the municipality of Stilfs in South Tyrol. As part of this exchange, artist Marie Capesius had the opportunity to spend a month in Stilfs, immersing herself in the place, its surroundings and its history. In return, Italian artist Karin Schmuck was invited to Luxembourg for a residency.

This artistic exchange culminated in two simultaneous exhibitions in Clervaux, where the artists presented the works they had created during their respective residencies. It was particularly interesting to observe how differently the two artists perceived these places, which were initially unfamiliar to them, how they approached them and how they translated their impressions into their artistic work.

The two exhibitions in Clervaux not only highlighted the artists’ individual approaches but also opened up a fascinating dialogue between two places, two perspectives and two different ways of working. This exchange was precisely what made the project so compelling. It demonstrated how a change of location can generate new ideas and how differently artists can experience, interpret and represent a place through their work.

Supporting artists in the development of new projects is an essential part of my work and something I care deeply about. For me, discussions, ongoing exchanges and collective reflection on ideas and concepts play a particularly important role. I want to encourage artists in their projects, support their development and, where appropriate, offer new ideas and perspectives.

I particularly enjoy visiting artists in their studios, observing their working processes and following the development of their work over an extended period. Depending on their needs, I also provide practical support, whether by writing exhibition texts, connecting them with curators or facilitating relationships with other institutions and figures in the art world.

I see my work not simply as collaboration on individual projects, but as a long-term process that extends beyond particular exhibitions. Maintaining contact with artists, following their development and continuing our collaboration after a project has ended are especially important to me.
